REVISEThe even-arm freezing induction contains an adjacency error and must be replaced. There is a short repair using the already frozen chamber, and it restores freezing for arbitrary simultaneous bundles. With that repair, the family construction, exact receiver charge, terminal-strip budget, and perpendicular separator argument work under the stated hypotheses.The final theorem also needs an explicit justification that the initial “thin” alternative passes to surviving endpoint components. The granted theorem about final thin receivers does not, by itself, supply that inheritance property. There is also a contradictory sentence in the sharpness paragraph to delete.I found no counterexample to the geometric separator under the stated requirements of one fixed physical tiling, endpoint-free strips, and distinct complete endpoint components.1. Required repair to simultaneous freezingThe retained-mate principle is correct. Fix an arbitrary feasible simultaneous bundle and let  $S$  be its set of promoted endpoints. Then
$$z\notin S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m(z)\text{ remains occupied}.$$
Indeed, the only way to delete  $m(z)$  is to use its matching edge with  $z$  promoted. “Remains occupied” can mean that  $m(z)$  itself becomes selected; this is sufficient for the argument.The descending odd-arm induction works. The terminal odd endpoint has two prescribed selected neighbors. Subsequently, for odd  $j\le L-2$ , the already unpromotable  $p_{j+2}^c$  forces its mate  $p_{j+1}^c$  to remain occupied, providing the second occupied neighbor of  $p_j^c$ .The chamber wave also works: $z_1=(0,0)$  sees the prescribed support  $(0,-1)$  and the retained mate  $m(z_0)=(1,0)$ .The recurrence for  $z_{j+2}$  starts at  $j=0$ : in particular,  $z_2=(1,1)$  sees  $m(z_0)=(1,0)$  and  $m(z_1)=(0,1)$ .The two claimed retained mates are distinct adjacent vertices at every subsequent step.Because  $w$  is even, reflection preserves the actual matching and supplies the other checkerboard-color wave.The error occurs in the final even-arm induction. The note says that  $p_2^c$  sees  $m(p_1^c)=(1,c)$ . But
$$p_2^c=(3,c),$$
so those vertices are two lattice steps apart. Likewise, for even  $j\ge4$ ,
$$m(p_{j-1}^c)=p_{j-2}^c$$
is two steps from  $p_j^c$ , not an occupied neighbor of it.Replace that passage by the following:Once the chamber has been frozen, its endpoint  $(1,c)$  cannot be promoted. Consequently its mate  $p_1^c$  remains occupied. The vertex  $p_2^c$  sees  $p_1^c$  and its prescribed inside selected support, so  $p_2^c$  cannot be promoted.Now let  $j=4,6,\ldots,2h$ . The previously frozen endpoint  $p_{j-2}^c$  has retained mate
$$m(p_{j-2}^c)=p_{j-1}^c.$$
This mate is adjacent to  $p_j^c$ . Together with the inside selected support, it prevents promotion of  $p_j^c$ .This works also at  $h=1$ , when only the even-arm base step is needed.All these statements concern the same arbitrary simultaneous bundle. After every endpoint of  $H$  has been shown unpromotable, no matching edge of  $H$  can be used, because using it would promote one of its endpoints. Thus the entire source and its actual matching survive unchanged. Exterior promotions do not affect this conclusion.2. All-width/all-depth feasibility and exact receiver chargeBaseline and saturated fillingThe baseline support count  $4h+6$ , mutual nonadjacency, intended endpoint incidences, and perfect matching of  $H$  check for every even  $w\ge8$  and  $h\ge1$ .For the band filling, it is useful to write the selected columns as
$$U=\{2\}\cup\{5,7,\ldots,w-3\}$$
in the upper row, and
$$D=\{1,3,4\}\cup\{6,8,\ldots,w-2\}$$
in the lower row. These sets partition  $\{1,\ldots,w-2\}$ .This proves the needed feasibility assertions uniformly:There is no vertical selected adjacency within a band, since each column contains exactly one selected vertex.There is no vertical selected adjacency between successive bands, since the lower selected columns are disjoint from the next upper selected columns.Upper selected vertices have no horizontal selected neighbor.The only horizontal selected adjacency is the lower-row pair in columns  $3,4$ .For  $w\ge8$ , neither member of that pair touches an arm endpoint.The lower boundary selections in columns  $1,w-2$  are exactly the prescribed inside supports. Each has its arm endpoint as its sole occupied neighbor.Upper selections in the first band can touch chamber endpoints, but have no selected neighbor.The minimum allowed width  $w=8$  causes no degeneration: there are three tiles, and the exceptional lower pair remains separated from both arms.With the corrected freezing proof, the displayed configuration is terminal, since  $P=H$  and no source endpoint can be promoted.The selected count correctly accounts for the inside supports already included in the band patterns:
$$|T|=(4h+6)+h(w-2)-2h=hw+6.$$
Consequently,
$$|T|+|M|=(h+1)w+2h+7,$$
and the stated rectangular deficit is exactly
$$(h+4)(w+8)-\bigl((h+1)w+2h+7\bigr)
=3w+6h+25.$$
Original corrected receiver chargeThe receiver counts are correct:Receiver portionPhysical tilesSelected verticesChamber $w/2+1$  $2$ Nonterminal arm tiles $2h$  $2h$ Terminal arm tiles $2$  $4$ Total $w/2+2h+3$  $2h+6$ Every remaining corner of these tiles is either a prescribed endpoint or forced blank by a selected support already adjacent to its intended endpoint. Thus an arbitrary feasible completion cannot insert another endpoint or selected vertex into an unaccounted receiver corner.Moreover, every actual matching edge of  $H$  has both endpoint tiles in this receiver. Under the granted original transfer ledger, all matching-transfer corrections therefore cancel internally. There is no foreign endpoint in these tiles through which an exterior matching transfer could enter.The whole receiver charge is consequently exactly
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho(R_H)
&=(2h+6)+\frac{2w+4h+2}{2}
      -2\left(\frac w2+2h+3\right)\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}$$
This is a calculation in the original ledger, including its corrections.Each band tile has two selected vertices and no endpoint, so its original charge is zero. Thus adjoining any collection of the displayed  $B_s$  leaves the combined charge equal to  $+1$ .3. The saturated-band obstruction is valid, with a precise scopeThe construction establishes the following quantified statement:
$$\forall k\ge1,\ \exists h\ge k$$
such that the source is completely frozen, its receiver has charge  $+1$ , and all tiles of  $B_0,\ldots,B_{k-1}$  have charge zero. In fact, all  $h$  displayed nonterminal bands are saturated.Therefore a payment rule restricted to these bands cannot supply the necessary deficit. This includes every rule restricted to a fixed-depth prefix of complete nonterminal inward bands.The sentence“refutes every rule that always pays the receiver using a fixed number of complete inward bands”should explicitly preserve that restriction. A bound on the number of chosen bands does not itself bound how far away they may be chosen. Section 3 pays using one entire terminal strip whose position depends on the arm length.A precise replacement would be:For every fixed  $k$ , a rule restricted to the first  $k$  complete nonterminal inward bands cannot guarantee payment. More generally, in the displayed construction, no selection of the bands  $B_0,\ldots,B_{h-1}$  supplies any deficit.If “inward bands” is reserved strictly for the defined  $B_s$ , the existing claim has this valid interpretation. Making that convention explicit removes the potential overstatement. The note’s express reservation about other exterior donors and other bounded-radius methods is appropriate.4. Terminal-strip budget: correct; sharpness paragraph needs one deletionThe four boundary blankness deductions are valid.For example, the support  $(r-1,1)$  exists because  $r-1=2h+1$  is the row of the last even-indexed arm endpoint. It already sees  $(r-1,0)$ , so feasibility forces  $(r,1)$  blank. The axial support similarly forces  $(r+1,1)$  blank. Reflection gives the other boundary column.The remaining vertices partition into the shifted unit squares with column pairs
$$(2,3),(4,5),\ldots,(w-4,w-3).$$
Any three selected corners of a unit square give one selected corner two selected neighbors. Hence every such square contains at most two selected vertices, and
$$|T\cap F_H|\le 2\frac{w-4}{2}=w-4.$$
The endpoint-free assumption then permits the original charge calculation
$$\rho(F_H)
=|T\cap F_H|-2\frac{w-2}{2}
\le-2.$$
The shifted squares are only a partition for counting vertices. They introduce no tile reassignment or matching-transfer issue.The contradictory sharpness sentenceThe sharpness paragraph initially claims that the proposed vertical pairs have no extra occupied neighbor “in the baseline with saturated inward bands.” That clause is false, although the paragraph subsequently corrects it.For every allowed width, the proposed selected vertex  $(r,3)$  has:its selected vertical partner  $(r+1,3)$ ; andthe selected vertex  $(r-1,3)$  from the last saturated band.Thus it would have two occupied neighbors.Delete the contrary clause and state directly:The sharp filling is incompatible with the saturated-band filling. Use it with the sparse forced-support baseline.With that baseline, the vertical pairs in columns  $3,5,\ldots,w-3$  are feasible and attain  $w-4$  selected vertices. The sharpness claim then stands exactly as intended.5. The disjoint-strip proof survives the geometric auditParallel stripsThe interval argument is correct for physical tile intervals.For two overlapping unequal integer intervals, an immediately exterior boundary tile of one lies in the other. That tile contains the first source’s tip endpoint, contradicting the endpoint-free condition of the other strip.If the intervals are equal, the corresponding tips occupy the same inward-facing column of each boundary tile. Their row coordinates either coincide or differ by one. Thus the two sources share a  $P$ -vertex or have adjacent  $P$ -vertices. Both possibilities contradict their being distinct complete endpoint components.This also covers opposite-facing parallel sources.Perpendicular stripsThe key inference is justified by alignment with the same physical tiling. An intersection of the two strips contains a whole common physical tile. Therefore:the vertical strip’s entire two-column band lies in columns  $1,\ldots,w-2$ ; andits row interval contains both  $r$  and  $r+1$ .If its tips are  $(u,c)$  and  $(v,c)$ , with  $u<v$ , this gives
$$c\in\{1,\ldots,w-2\},\qquad
u\le r-1,\qquad v\ge r+2.$$
The initial cases are sound:If  $u\le0$ , the vertical endpoint-free strip contains  $(1,c)$ , which is a chamber endpoint of  $H$ .If  $u=1$ , the upper tip itself belongs to  $H$ .Hence a remaining candidate must have  $2\le u\le r-1$ , putting its upper tip in  $I$ .The separator can be made completely explicit. For
$$I=\{2,\ldots,r-1\}\times\{1,\ldots,w-2\},$$
its outside nearest-neighbor boundary is
$$\partial I=
\bigl(\{1,r\}\times\{1,\ldots,w-2\}\bigr)
\;\cup\;
\bigl(\{2,\ldots,r-1\}\times\{0,w-1\}\bigr).$$
Every vertex of this boundary belongs to  $H$  or  $F_H$ :row  $1$  belongs to the chamber;columns  $0,w-1$  belong to the arms;row  $r$ , between the arms, belongs to the endpoint-free strip.Now take a  $P$ -path in the second source connecting its tips and consider its first exit from  $I$ . The exit vertex belongs to  $\partial I$ . If it belongs to  $H$ , the two complete endpoint components coincide. If it belongs to  $F_H$ , it cannot be a  $P$ -vertex.These exhaust all exits. In particular, a nearest-neighbor path cannot escape diagonally through a corner.No additional disjoint-neighborhood hypothesis is needed. The existing completeness and tiling hypotheses are doing the necessary work. Adding the explicit boundary formula or first-exit formulation would make that dependence easier to inspect, but the geometric argument itself has no gap.6. Final initial-pair theorem: valid after the freezing repair and inheritance justificationTerminalization and preservationEvery nonempty promotion bundle removes at least one matching edge and preserves  $|T|+|M|$ . Thus repeated feasible promotions terminate after finitely many steps.Under the corrected freezing lemma:every prescribed source retains all its endpoints and its actual matching;every prescribed selected support remains selected;the endpoint set only decreases;a prescribed complete initial component remains complete;other endpoint components can only split or shrink;each initially endpoint-free terminal strip remains endpoint-free.No enlargement or merging of endpoint components is possible through endpoint deletion.The one dependency application needing clarification“Contains at most one  $P$ -square” is hereditary: deleting endpoints cannot create a new fully occupied  $P$ -square.The corresponding assertion for thin cannot be checked from the inlined note because “thin” is not defined here. The granted statement
$$\text{final component thin}\Longrightarrow \rho\le0$$
does not establish
$$\text{initial component thin}\Longrightarrow
\text{every surviving component thin}.$$
Add a definition-based argument or an explicit citation for closure under the endpoint deletions used by promotion bundles. At minimum, every surviving component descending from an initial thin component must belong to the granted nonpositive-receiver class.If the adopted definition of thin is already hereditary, this is a short dependency clarification. Otherwise the initial thin branch requires an additional hypothesis. It should not be inferred solely from the final receiver theorem.Also make explicit that  $B$  counts distinct complete initial endpoint components, as required by the disjoint-strip lemma.Exact ledger applicationAt the terminal pair, the granted tile-owner lemma makes the complete endpoint receivers disjoint. The terminal strips are mutually disjoint by Section 4. Because they are unions of endpoint-free physical tiles, they lie outside every receiver under the granted receiver convention.Let  $t_Q$  denote the final selected count in a physical tile. For every remaining no- $P$  tile,
$$t_Q\le2,$$
by the same three-corners argument used above.The original ledger therefore groups exactly as claimed:
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{mn}{2}-|T_0|-|M_0|
={}&
\sum_{\text{nonprescribed }C}-\rho(R_C)\\
&+\sum_{\text{prescribed }H}
   \bigl(-1-\rho(F_H)\bigr)\\
&+\sum_{Q\in Z\setminus F}(2-t_Q).
\end{aligned}$$
Each term has the asserted sign:nonprescribed whole-receiver deficits are nonnegative by the granted theorem, once inheritance is justified;each prescribed source and its strip contribute
$$-1-\rho(F_H)\ge1;$$
every remaining no- $P$  tile contributes  $2-t_Q\ge0$ .Thus
$$|T_0|+|M_0|\le \frac{mn}{2}-B.$$
Objective preservation correctly transfers this terminal ledger conclusion to the initial pair. No physical tile is spent twice.The coefficient comparison is also algebraically correct: the bound implies
$$|T_0|+\frac56|M_0|
\le \frac{mn}{2}-B-\frac16|M_0|.$$
Required revisions: replace the even-arm induction; justify the inheritance of the thin class; remove the false saturated-baseline sharpness clause; and state the band-obstruction scope explicitly. The geometric separator and the terminal-strip payment mechanism require no further separation hypothesis.
